n: Moved by Judah’s plea, Joseph could hold back no longer. He sent all the Egyptians out so he could reveal himself privately to his brothers.
Joseph wept so loudly that the Egyptians outside—and soon Pharaoh’s household—heard it.
“I am Joseph.” His first question is about his father. The brothers were stunned speechless, even terrified, standing before the brother they had wronged.
Joseph draws them close and names the painful truth plainly—“whom ye sold”—not to accuse, but so forgiveness can be real.
Joseph urges them not to be consumed by self-blame, because God turned their evil act into a way to save lives. This is one of scripture’s great statements of God’s providence.

f.w: God did send me before you to preserve life

n: Only two years of famine had passed; five more remained with no plowing or harvest.
God sent Joseph ahead to preserve a remnant of the covenant family and bring about a great deliverance—a foreshadowing of Christ, rejected by His own, who becomes their Savior.
Joseph sees God’s hand above his brothers’ choices. “Father to Pharaoh” was an Egyptian title for a chief adviser.

f.g: a title for a trusted chief counselor

n: Joseph urges them to hurry and bring Jacob to Egypt without delay.
The family could settle in Goshen, fertile land in the eastern Nile Delta, near Joseph and suited to their flocks.

f.g: a region of pastureland in the northeastern Nile Delta

n: Joseph promises to provide for the whole family through the remaining five years of famine.
Joseph points out they can see and hear him speaking directly in their own language—no interpreter—proof it is truly him.

f.w: it is my mouth that speaketh unto you

n: He wants his father to know of his honor in Egypt and to come quickly.
Joseph and Benjamin embraced and wept together—the reunion of Rachel’s two sons.

f.w: fell upon his brother Benjamin's neck

n: Joseph kissed all his brothers and wept with them. Only then could they talk with him—the silence of fear was broken by forgiveness.

f.w: after that his brethren talked with him

n: News of the reunion reached Pharaoh’s palace, and Pharaoh and his officials were pleased.
Pharaoh tells Joseph to send his brothers home to bring the family back.
Pharaoh generously offers the best of Egypt to Jacob’s family.

f.g: the richest produce of the land

n: Pharaoh even provides wagons to carry the women and children—a rare luxury in Canaan.
Don’t worry about leaving belongings behind, Pharaoh says—the best of Egypt will be yours.

f.g: don’t be concerned about your possessions

n: The brothers set out with wagons and supplies as Pharaoh commanded.
Joseph gave each brother new clothing—fitting, since a robe had once caused their division—but gave Benjamin extra silver and five sets of clothes.

f.g: compare the twenty pieces for which Joseph was sold

n: Joseph sent his father twenty donkeys loaded with Egypt’s best goods and food for the journey.
Joseph adds a brotherly warning: don’t quarrel on the way. He knew they might be tempted to blame one another over the past.
The brothers traveled home to Canaan and their father.
They told Jacob that Joseph was alive and ruling Egypt. Jacob’s heart went numb—he could not believe it after twenty years of grief.

f.g: his heart went numb, stood still

n: As they repeated Joseph’s words and he saw the wagons, Jacob’s spirit came back to life. The evidence matched the message.
Now called Israel again, the patriarch declares: “It is enough”—Joseph lives, and I will see him before I die.
